topic: Why commercial kitchen exhaust systems get loud

slides.headline: If the kitchen roars, the system is telling you something.
slides.subline: Noise is usually resistance, balance, or a fan working too hard.

slides.title: Three common causes

items.title: Duct velocity
items.text: Air forced through a tight duct gets loud before it gets weak.

items.title: Fan balance
items.text: Grease or a damaged blade makes the whole unit hum.

items.title: Mounting
items.text: A fan bolted straight to structure sends noise into the building.

slides.note_text: A new hum, a rattle at start-up, a pitch that climbs.

slides.title: What actually quietens it
slides.intro: None of it is padding stuck to the ceiling.

items.title: Sizing
items.text: A fan running inside its range is quieter than one at its limit.

items.title: Isolation
items.text: Rubber mounts and flexible connections break the path.

items.title: Route
items.text: Smooth bends and a straight outlet do more than insulation.

slides.note_text: Ask for it at design stage, not after handover.

slides.headline: A loud kitchen is a symptom, not a personality.
slides.subline: We trace the noise before we sell a new fan.

caption_en:
Some kitchens are loud because they are busy. Others are loud because the exhaust is working against itself.

Three things cause most of it. Air pushed through a duct that is too tight. A fan that has gone out of balance, usually from grease or a damaged blade. And a unit bolted straight onto the structure, so every vibration becomes building noise.

A bigger fan rarely fixes any of those. It usually makes the first two worse. We measure the route, check the fan, and treat the mounting before recommending equipment.
